profile.feeling: Everyday and warm: shared meals (zusammen essen) are a social ritual.

senses.def: to have a meal, to dine (essen gehen = to eat out)

examples.text: Isst du Fleisch?

examples.text: Er isst jeden Tag einen Apfel.
examples.tr: He eats an apple every day.

examples.text: Zum Frühstück esse ich Brot mit Käse.
examples.tr: For breakfast I eat bread and cheese.

examples.text: Wir essen um sieben Uhr zu Abend.
examples.tr: We have dinner at seven.

examples.text: Am Wochenende gehen wir essen.

phrases.meaning: How food looks matters.

to eat with others, join in

to ingest, take (food) – medical or official language
to tuck in, eat heartily – playful
neutral for animals; said of people it means eating greedily, like an animal

etymology.text: From Middle High German ëȥȥen, from Old High German ëȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *etan, from Proto-Germanic *etaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ed-. Cognate with Dutch eten, English eat, Swedish äta; non-Germanic cognates include Latin edō and Russian есть (jestʹ).

funFacts: Animals do not “essen” in German, they “fressen” – using fressen for a person is rude or jokey.
The past participle is gegessen, with an extra -ge-; the old form gessen is obsolete.
Greek τρώω, Russian есть / кушать, Turkish yemek: Russian есть is a cousin of essen and English eat (Indo-European *h₁ed-).
pitfalls: Stem vowel e → i: du isst, er isst (not *esst); du isst and er isst are spelled the same.
Past tense with ß: ich aß, wir aßen.
du isst and er isst look the same: the s of the ending melts into the ss of the stem (not *du issst).
Imperative: Iss! (du – the i stays, no -e) – Esst! (ihr) – Essen Sie! (polite).
subtleties: Soup is eaten in German (Suppe essen), not drunk.

profile.feeling: Coffee breaks, beer gardens, toasts – and, without an object, the drinking of alcohol.

senses.def: to drink alcohol (habitually) – used without an object: Er trinkt.
auf jemanden/etwas trinken: to drink to, to toast

examples.text: Was trinkst du? – Ein Wasser, bitte.
examples.tr: What are you drinking? – A water, please.

examples.text: Morgens trinke ich immer Tee.
examples.tr: In the morning I always drink tea.

examples.text: Sein Vater trinkt seit Jahren nicht mehr.
examples.tr: His father hasn't drunk alcohol for years.

examples.text: Wir trinken auf das Brautpaar!
examples.tr: Let's drink to the bride and groom!

collocations.tr: to drink coffee (also: to have a coffee break)
to drink a glass of water

phrases.meaning: a toast

particleVerbs.tr: to raise one's glass to someone

synonyms.nuance: to slurp, sip noisily
to take a tiny sip
neutral for animals; for people: to drink a lot, especially alcohol – crude

etymology.text: From Middle High German trinken, from Old High German trinkan (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan. Cognates include Dutch drinken, English drink, Swedish dricka and Gothic 𐌳𐍂𐌹𐌲𐌺𐌰𐌽 (drigkan).

funFacts: Kaffee und Kuchen: in Germany “Kaffee trinken” in the afternoon is a small meal with cake, not just a drink.
das Trinkgeld (“drink money”) is the German word for a tip in a restaurant or a taxi.
trinken and English drink are the same Germanic verb (Dutch drinken, Swedish dricka).
pitfalls: Without an object, Er trinkt usually means “he drinks (too much alcohol)”.
Strong verb: trinken – trank – getrunken (not *getrinkt).
Regular in the present: ich trinke, du trinkst, er trinkt – the vowel changes only in the past (trank, getrunken).
Imperative: Trink! (or Trinke!) – Trinkt! – Trinken Sie!
subtleties: Wollen wir einen Kaffee trinken gehen? is an invitation to meet and talk, not only to drink coffee.

profile.feeling: Shops, markets, the Saturday shopping list.

senses.def: to buy (something) for someone: jemandem etwas kaufen

examples.text: Ich kaufe Gemüse immer auf dem Markt.
examples.tr: I always buy vegetables at the market.

to get, fetch – focus on obtaining, not on paying
to go shopping (for fun) – an anglicism

etymology.text: From Middle High German koufen, from Old High German koufōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kaupōn, an early borrowing of Latin caupō (“innkeeper, petty trader”). Related to English cheap and Swedish köpa.

funFacts: The Danish cognate is in Copenhagen: København = “merchants' harbour”.
pitfalls: einkaufen is “to go shopping” in general; kaufen needs an object: Ich kaufe Brot. / Ich gehe einkaufen.
Regular verb: ich kaufe, du kaufst, er kauft, wir kaufen, ihr kauft, sie kaufen – no vowel change.
Imperative: Kauf! (or Kaufe!) – Kauft! – Kaufen Sie!
subtleties: Kauf mir was! – with a dative, kaufen means buying for someone.

profile.feeling: Liking food, music, people – friendly, not passionate.

senses.def: would like (the forms möchte, möchtest, möchten, möchtet – Konjunktiv II, used like a present)
may (concession or possibility): Das mag sein.

examples.text: Ich mag Tomaten, aber keine Gurken.
examples.tr: I like tomatoes, but not cucumbers.

examples.text: Magst du Jazz?
examples.tr: Do you like jazz?

examples.text: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.
examples.tr: I'd like a coffee, please.

examples.text: Das mag sein, aber ich glaube es nicht.
examples.tr: That may be, but I don't believe it.

examples.text: Möchten Sie Tee oder Kaffee?
examples.tr: Would you like tea or coffee?

collocations.tr: not to like something at all

phrases.meaning: a concession: that may well be true (but …)

synonyms.nuance: to be fond of (a person) – warmer than mögen
to love – much stronger for people; for things it is emphatic (Ich liebe Pizza!)
mostly negated: Ich kann ihn nicht leiden = I can't stand him

etymology.text: From Middle High German mugen, from Old High German mugan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą, from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ-. Compare Dutch mogen, English may. The sense “to like” developed in the 16th century from negated nicht mögen (“not to be able to” → “not to like doing”); the old sense “to be able to” fell out of use in the 17th century.

funFacts: mögen is a cousin of English may and might: it once meant “to be able”.
Greek θα ήθελα, Russian я хотел бы, English I would like: German packs the polite “would like” into one word, möchte.
pitfalls: For activities German prefers gern + verb: Ich schwimme gern (I like swimming), rather than Ich mag schwimmen.
No ending in ich mag / er mag; vowel change ö → a in the singular.
möchte is a form of mögen used as “would like”: ich möchte, du möchtest, er/sie möchte, wir möchten, ihr möchtet, sie/Sie möchten – the er-form has no -t (er möchte, not *er möchtet).
Ich mag Kaffee = I like coffee (in general); Ich möchte einen Kaffee = I would like a coffee (now).
subtleties: Ich mag dich (I like you) – Ich hab dich lieb (I'm fond of you, family and friends) – Ich liebe dich (I love you).
möchte (would like) is the polite way to ask for something; Ich will … can sound demanding.

profile.feeling: Direct will and intention – honest, but can sound blunt in a shop.

senses.def: to want (something or to do something)
to claim (Er will es nicht gewusst haben = he claims not to have known)
to be about to, to intend

examples.text: Willst du eine Tomate?
examples.tr: Do you want a tomato?

examples.text: Die Kinder wollen heute Pizza essen.
examples.tr: The children want to eat pizza today.

examples.text: Er will nichts davon gewusst haben.
examples.tr: He claims to have known nothing about it.

examples.text: Ich wollte gerade gehen, als du angerufen hast.
examples.tr: I was just about to leave when you called.

phrases.text: Wer nicht will, der hat schon.
phrases.meaning: if you turn down an offer, that's your loss

particleVerbs.tr: to want to come along (colloquial: Willst du mit?)

synonyms.nuance: would like – the polite choice when asking for something
to wish, desire – service language: Was wünschen Sie?
to feel like (doing) something

etymology.text: From Middle High German wollen, wöllen, wellen, from Old High German wollen, wellen, from a blend of Proto-West Germanic *willjan and *walljan, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną and *waljaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. Compare Dutch willen, English will.

funFacts: English “will” was once “to want”, too – that sense survives in “if you will” and in “willing”.
Greek θέλω να πιω τσάι, Russian хочу пить чай and Turkish çay içmek istiyorum keep the two verbs side by side; German splits them around the object: Ich will Tee trinken.
pitfalls: False friend: German Ich will = I want, not “I will”. The future is werden: Ich werde kommen.
Ich will einen Kaffee can sound rude when ordering – say Ich möchte … or Ich hätte gern …
ich will and er will have no ending – like all modal verbs (ich kann, ich muss, ich mag).
A second verb goes to the very end as an infinitive: Ich will Tee trinken. (not *Ich will trinken Tee)
subtleties: Like other modal verbs, wollen often drops a verb of motion: Ich will nach Hause. Willst du mit?

profile.feeling: The stove, the smell of soup, a family cooking together – kochen is everyday warm food.

senses.def: to boil (water boils; to boil eggs, potatoes); to make (coffee, tea)
to seethe, to boil with anger (figurative)

examples.text: Ich koche heute eine Suppe.
examples.tr: I’m cooking a soup today.

examples.text: Mein Vater kocht sehr gut.
examples.tr: My father cooks very well.

examples.text: Wer kocht heute das Abendessen?
examples.tr: Who is cooking dinner today?

examples.text: Das Wasser kocht schon.
examples.tr: The water is already boiling.

examples.text: Er kocht vor Wut.
examples.tr: He is boiling with rage.

collocations.tr: to cook food, make a meal

phrases.meaning: too many cooks spoil the broth

phrases.text: Hier wird auch nur mit Wasser gekocht.
phrases.tr: Here, too, they only cook with water.
phrases.meaning: they are no better than anyone else

phrases.text: Es wird nichts so heiß gegessen, wie es gekocht wird.
phrases.tr: Nothing is eaten as hot as it is cooked.
phrases.meaning: things are rarely as bad as they first seem

synonyms.nuance: to prepare (a dish) – recipes, menus
to fry or roast – one way of cooking, in fat or in the oven
to bake – bread and cake, in the oven; not a synonym of kochen but its neighbour
to sizzle, to fry something up – playful

etymology.text: From Middle High German kochen, from Old High German kohhōn, from Proto-West Germanic *kokōn (“to cook”).

funFacts: der Koch (the cook) and die Küche (the kitchen) – like English cook and kitchen – come from Latin coquus and coquīna.
kochen means both “to cook” and “to boil” (Das Wasser kocht); Greek separates μαγειρεύω (to cook) and βράζω (to boil), as English separates cook and boil.
pitfalls: Regular verb: ich koche, du kochst, er kocht – no vowel change.
kochen is cooking on the stove; in the oven bread and cake are gebacken (backen), meat is gebraten (braten).
subtleties: Kaffee kochen and Tee kochen mean “to make coffee / tea”, even with a machine.
Used alone, Ich koche means “I’m cooking (a meal)”: Heute koche ich!

profile.feeling: The heart of the German table: dark, crusty, many kinds – the evening meal Abendbrot is named after it.

senses.def: a loaf of bread; a slice of bread with something on it (countable)

examples.text: Ich kaufe jeden Morgen frisches Brot.
examples.tr: I buy fresh bread every morning.

examples.text: Am Abend essen wir Brot mit Käse.
examples.tr: In the evening we eat bread and cheese.

examples.text: Kannst du zwei Brote vom Bäcker mitbringen?

examples.text: Er verdient sein Brot als Taxifahrer.

collocations.tr: slice of bread and butter, sandwich

phrases.text: Der Mensch lebt nicht vom Brot allein.
phrases.tr: Man does not live by bread alone.
phrases.meaning: people need more than food (Matthew 4:4)

phrases.text: Wes Brot ich ess, des Lied ich sing.
phrases.tr: Whose bread I eat, his song I sing.
phrases.meaning: you are loyal to whoever pays you
to earn one’s living

synonyms.nuance: a whole loaf (ein Laib Brot) – only the shape, not the food
a slice of bread with a topping – Berlin and the north
the same in Saxony and Thuringia

etymology.text: From Middle High German brōt, from Old High German brōt, from Proto-West Germanic *braud, from Proto-Germanic *braudą, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrew- (“to seethe, to boil”). Originally “what has been fermented, leaven”. It replaced the older Laib (“loaf”), the more common term in Old High German.

funFacts: Russian хлеб comes from the old Germanic word for bread (*hlaibaz) – the word that lives on in German Laib and English loaf.
German bread culture (Deutsche Brotkultur) is on Germany’s national list of intangible cultural heritage, with thousands of registered kinds of bread.
pitfalls: Uncountable for the food (Ich esse Brot), countable for a loaf (ein Brot, zwei Brote).
das Brot is neuter; a bread roll is das Brötchen (regionally Semmel, Schrippe), not *kleines Brot.
subtleties: Abendbrot (“evening bread”) is the evening meal in the north and east – traditionally cold, with bread, cheese and cold meat.

profile.feeling: Breakfast rolls, fondue, the cheese board – and, colloquially, nonsense.

examples.text: Ich esse gern Käse zum Frühstück.
examples.tr: I like eating cheese for breakfast.

examples.text: Im Supermarkt kaufe ich Käse und Milch.
examples.tr: At the supermarket I buy cheese and milk.

examples.text: Ach, das ist doch Käse!
examples.tr: Oh, that’s nonsense!

phrases.meaning: that is nonsense
cheese ends a meal

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym: Käse is the only general word; single cheeses have their own names (Gouda, Emmentaler, Quark – fresh curd cheese).

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German kæse, from Old High German kāsi, from Proto-West Germanic *kāsī (“cheese”), borrowed from Latin cāseus.

funFacts: Käse, English cheese and Spanish queso all come from Latin cāseus; Greek τυρί, Russian сыр and Turkish peynir have other origins.
pitfalls: der Käse is masculine (Greek το τυρί is neuter, Russian сыр masculine).
Plural Käse (kinds of cheese), dative plural Käsen; genitive des Käses.
subtleties: Uncountable for the food: Ich mag Käse. ein Käse is a whole cheese or a kind of cheese.

profile.feeling: Boiled eggs at Sunday breakfast, painted eggs at Easter.

senses.def: egg (food; also of birds and other animals)

examples.text: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Ei.
examples.tr: For breakfast I eat an egg.

examples.text: Kaufst du bitte zehn Eier?
examples.tr: Will you buy ten eggs, please?

examples.text: Für den Kuchen brauchen wir drei Eier.
examples.tr: We need three eggs for the cake.

phrases.tr: as if peeled out of the egg
phrases.meaning: immaculately dressed
a surprisingly simple solution

phrases.text: sich gleichen wie ein Ei dem anderen
phrases.tr: to be like one egg to the other
phrases.meaning: to be as alike as two peas in a pod

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: Ei is the only word for egg.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German ei and Old High German ei, from Proto-West Germanic *aij, from Proto-Germanic *ajją, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm. Cognate with Yiddish איי (ey), Dutch ei, English ey and egg, Danish æg.

funFacts: English once had its own word ey (plural eyren), the twin of German Ei; egg came from Old Norse. In 1490 the printer William Caxton told of a merchant who asked a woman for “eggys” and was told she spoke no French – she only knew “eyren”.
Ei, Latin ovum, Ancient Greek ᾠόν (modern αυγό) and Russian яйцо all go back to one Indo-European word for egg.
pitfalls: Plural Eier (dative Eiern): ein Ei, zwei Eier.
In slang Eier means testicles – Eier haben = to have guts. Harmless in the kitchen, but jokes are everywhere.
subtleties: das Ei is neuter, like Greek το αυγό; Russian яйцо is neuter too.
Ostereier (Easter eggs) are painted or made of chocolate; der Osterhase (Easter bunny) brings them.

profile.feeling: Sunday roast and the butcher’s counter – and a daily question for vegetarians.

senses.def: flesh (of a body); the soft inside of a fruit (Fruchtfleisch)

examples.text: Mein Bruder isst kein Fleisch.
examples.tr: My brother doesn’t eat meat.

examples.text: Wir kaufen das Fleisch beim Metzger.
examples.tr: We buy the meat at the butcher’s.

examples.text: Heute gibt es Fleisch mit Kartoffeln.

examples.text: Der Dorn geht tief ins Fleisch.
examples.tr: The thorn goes deep into the flesh.

phrases.meaning: neither one thing nor the other
one’s own children

phrases.tr: to pass into flesh and blood
phrases.meaning: to become second nature

profile.synonymsNone: No general synonym: the kinds are compounds (Rindfleisch, Schweinefleisch, Hähnchenfleisch); Wurst is sausage, Braten a roast.

etymology.text: From Middle High German fleisch, vleisch, from Old High German fleisk, from Proto-West Germanic *flaiski.

funFacts: English splits meat and flesh and took beef, pork and mutton from Norman French; German keeps one word and builds compounds: Rindfleisch (cow meat = beef), Schweinefleisch (pig meat = pork).
Fleisch and English flesh are the same Germanic word.
pitfalls: No plural: kinds of meat are Fleischsorten.
das Fleisch is neuter; the butcher is der Metzger (south and west), der Fleischer (east) or der Schlachter (north).
subtleties: Many Germans do not count fish as Fleisch: Ich esse kein Fleisch, nur Fisch.

profile.feeling: Fish on Fridays, fish rolls at the North Sea, trout from a mountain stream.

senses.def: Fische (plural): Pisces, the sign of the zodiac

examples.text: Am Freitag essen wir oft Fisch.
examples.tr: On Fridays we often eat fish.

examples.text: Ich koche heute Fisch mit Reis.
examples.tr: Today I’m cooking fish with rice.

examples.text: Im See schwimmen viele Fische.

phrases.meaning: neither one thing nor the other
trifles, small fry

phrases.text: sich wie ein Fisch im Wasser fühlen
phrases.tr: to feel like a fish in water
phrases.meaning: to be completely in one’s element

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym in everyday use; kinds of fish have their own names (Lachs, Forelle, Thunfisch).

etymology.text: From Middle High German visch, from Old High German fisk, fisc, from Proto-West Germanic *fisk.

funFacts: Fisch and Latin piscis are the same Indo-European word: Germanic turned p into f, as in Vater – pater, Fuß – pes.
pitfalls: For the food, no article and no plural: Ich esse gern Fisch. einen Fisch is a whole fish.
der Fisch is masculine; plural Fische, dative plural Fischen.
subtleties: In German Fisch is usually not Fleisch: a person who eats fish but no meat says Ich esse kein Fleisch.

profile.feeling: Roast chicken from the grill van, chicken with rice – plain, popular food.

senses.def: chicken (as food: a whole roast or grilled chicken, or chicken meat)

examples.text: Heute gibt es Hähnchen mit Reis.
examples.tr: Today we’re having chicken with rice.

examples.text: Am Imbiss kaufen wir ein halbes Hähnchen.
examples.tr: At the snack bar we buy half a chicken.

examples.text: Ich koche ein Hähnchen für die ganze Familie.
examples.tr: I’m cooking a chicken for the whole family.

phrases.text: mit jemandem ein Hühnchen zu rupfen haben
phrases.tr: to have a little chicken to pluck with someone
phrases.meaning: to have a bone to pick with someone

synonyms.nuance: the live bird, a hen; as food in Hühnersuppe or Huhn mit Reis
little chicken – a bit homelier, same food
Bavaria and Austria: roast chicken (Brathendl)
eastern Germany, from GDR times
Switzerland

etymology.text: From Hahn (“rooster”) + -chen (diminutive).

funFacts: Hähnchen is literally “little rooster”, yet it names any chicken for the table. Greek κοτόπουλο (from κότα, hen) and Russian курица (hen) name the food after the hen instead.
pitfalls: Huhn is the live animal (a hen); for food Germans in Germany usually say Hähnchen: Ich esse Hähnchen.
The plural is the same as the singular: ein Hähnchen, zwei Hähnchen.
subtleties: Every noun in -chen is neuter: das Hähnchen, das Brötchen, das Mädchen – even though der Hahn is masculine.

profile.feeling: A side dish, rice pudding for children, and the staple of half the world.

examples.text: Wir essen heute Reis mit Gemüse.
examples.tr: Today we’re eating rice with vegetables.

examples.text: Ich koche den Reis zwanzig Minuten.
examples.tr: I cook the rice for twenty minutes.

examples.text: In Asien wird viel Reis angebaut.
examples.tr: A lot of rice is grown in Asia.

phrases.text: Da fällt in China ein Sack Reis um.
phrases.tr: A sack of rice falls over in China.
phrases.meaning: that is completely unimportant

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; kinds have their own names (Basmatireis, Milchreis, Risottoreis).

etymology.text: From Middle High German rīs, borrowed from Late Latin rīsum or rīsus, from Latin orȳza, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὄρῡζα (órūza).

funFacts: Reis came via Latin from Ancient Greek ὄρυζα – the word behind modern Greek ρύζι and English rice.
Chinese separates the plant 稻, the raw grain 米 and cooked rice 饭; German says Reis for all three.
pitfalls: der Reis (rice) – die Reise (journey) – reisen (to travel): three different words.
No plural in everyday use; kinds are Reissorten.
subtleties: Milchreis (rice cooked in milk with sugar and cinnamon) is eaten as a sweet main meal, not only as dessert.

profile.feeling: Grandmother’s chicken soup, a warm bowl in winter.

senses.def: thick fog, a pea-souper (die Suppe draußen)

examples.text: Im Winter koche ich oft Suppe.
examples.tr: In winter I often cook soup.

examples.text: Die Suppe ist sehr heiß.
examples.tr: The soup is very hot.

examples.text: Als Vorspeise nehmen wir eine Tomatensuppe.
examples.tr: As a starter we’ll have a tomato soup.

phrases.text: die Suppe auslöffeln, die man sich eingebrockt hat
phrases.tr: to spoon up the soup one has crumbled bread into
phrases.meaning: to face the consequences of one’s own actions
to spoil someone’s plans

phrases.text: ein Haar in der Suppe finden
phrases.tr: to find a hair in the soup
phrases.meaning: to find fault, to nitpick

synonyms.nuance: broth, clear soup
a thick one-pot soup-stew, a full meal
a little soup – homely; also in sein eigenes Süppchen kochen (to pursue one’s own agenda)

etymology.text: Borrowed from Middle Low German suppe, soppe, sope, which spread under the reinforcing influence of French soupe. Both from Proto-Germanic *supô, *suppô (“broth, sop”), related to German saufen (“to drink”).

funFacts: English supper comes from French souper, “to have soup” – the evening meal was soup.
Russian суп (from French soupe) and Greek σούπα belong to the same family of words.
pitfalls: Soup is eaten in German: Suppe essen, not *Suppe trinken.
die Suppe is feminine; plural Suppen.
subtleties: A Suppe in Germany is often a starter; an Eintopf is a whole meal in one pot.

profile.feeling: Fresh and light – the salad on the plate and the leafy plant it is made from.

senses.def: lettuce and related leaf vegetables (the plant)

examples.text: Als Vorspeise nehme ich einen gemischten Salat.
examples.tr: As a starter I’ll have a mixed salad.

examples.text: Ich mache einen Salat mit Tomaten und Gurken.
examples.tr: I’m making a salad with tomatoes and cucumbers.

examples.text: Ich kaufe einen Kopf Salat.
examples.tr: I'm buying a head of lettuce.

examples.text: Der Salat im Garten schießt schon.
examples.tr: The lettuce in the garden is already bolting.

examples.text: Zum Grillen mache ich einen Kartoffelsalat.
examples.tr: I'm making a potato salad for the barbecue.

phrases.meaning: Now we're in a mess! (when something predicted goes wrong)

synonyms.nuance: specifically round head lettuce (butterhead)
Austrian and southern German word for head lettuce
leaf salads in general

etymology.text: 15th century, from earlier Italian salata, a variant of insalata (“salted [dish]”), likely reinforced by Middle French salade.

funFacts: Salat goes back to salt (Latin sal): the first salads were salted greens.
Greek σαλάτα, Russian салат, Turkish salata and English salad are the same Romance word – of these, only German and Russian also use it for the lettuce plant.
pitfalls: Salat means both “lettuce” and “salad” – Kartoffelsalat has no lettuce at all.
Plural Salate; dative plural Salaten.
subtleties: For the plant it is often used without an article, like a mass noun: Salat waschen, Salat pflanzen.

profile.feeling: Apples and pears from the market stall – healthy, everyday fruit.

examples.text: Ich esse jeden Tag Obst.
examples.tr: I eat fruit every day.

examples.text: Auf dem Markt kaufen wir Obst und Gemüse.
examples.tr: At the market we buy fruit and vegetables.

examples.text: Zum Nachtisch gibt es Obst.
examples.tr: There’s fruit for dessert.

synonyms.nuance: fruits (plural of Frucht) – wider and more formal, also exotic fruit: Südfrüchte
a single fruit in botany; also figurative: die Früchte der Arbeit

etymology.text: From Middle High German obez, from Old High German obaz, from Proto-West Germanic *obaet.

funFacts: English fruit, Greek φρούτο and Russian фрукты come from Latin frūctus – in German that word is Frucht, while the fruit in the bowl is Obst.
pitfalls: Obst has no plural and no ein: say Obst (some fruit), ein Stück Obst (a piece of fruit) or name the fruit (ein Apfel).
das Obst is neuter.
subtleties: Obst means the sweet fruit of trees and bushes that you eat raw; tomatoes and cucumbers are botanically fruits but Gemüse in the kitchen.

profile.feeling: The most German fruit: apple strudel, apple juice, the apple tree in the garden.

examples.text: Ich esse jeden Tag einen Apfel.
examples.tr: I eat an apple every day.

examples.text: Wir kaufen ein Kilo Äpfel.
examples.tr: We’re buying a kilo of apples.

examples.text: Der Apfel ist rot und süß.
examples.tr: The apple is red and sweet.

phrases.text: Der Apfel fällt nicht weit vom Stamm.
phrases.tr: The apple does not fall far from the trunk.
phrases.meaning: children are like their parents

phrases.tr: to bite into the sour apple
phrases.meaning: to do something unpleasant that cannot be avoided
to compare things that cannot be compared

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; varieties have names (Boskop, Elstar, Gala).

etymology.text: From Middle High German apfel, from Old High German apful, from Proto-West Germanic *applu, from Proto-Germanic *apluz (compare Dutch appel, English apple), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ébōl.

funFacts: Apfel, English apple and Russian яблоко go back to the same Indo-European word; Greek μήλο and Turkish elma are unrelated.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: der Apfel – die Äpfel (dative den Äpfeln).
der Apfel is masculine (Greek το μήλο neuter, Russian яблоко neuter).
subtleties: In compounds it is Apfel-: Apfelsaft, Apfelkuchen, Apfelschorle (apple juice with sparkling water).

profile.feeling: Sweetness – in coffee, in cake; colloquially also diabetes.

examples.text: Trinkst du den Kaffee mit Zucker?
examples.tr: Do you take your coffee with sugar?

examples.text: Für den Kuchen brauche ich Zucker und Eier.
examples.tr: For the cake I need sugar and eggs.

examples.text: Mein Opa hat Zucker.
examples.tr: My grandpa has diabetes.

phrases.meaning: carrot and stick

phrases.tr: That is no licking of sugar.
phrases.meaning: it is no picnic, it is hard

profile.synonymsNone: No general synonym: Zucker is the only everyday word (Süßstoff is a different thing).

etymology.text: From Middle High German zucker, from Old High German zuckar, from early Italian zucchero, from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), from Persian شکر (šakar), from Sanskrit शर्करा (śárkarā, “grit, gravel; ground or candied sugar”).

funFacts: A travelling word: Sanskrit śarkarā → Persian šakar → Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar) → Italian zucchero → German Zucker. Greek ζάχαρη, Russian сахар, Turkish şeker, Hebrew סוּכָּר and English sugar come from the same source.
pitfalls: der Zucker is masculine; uncountable in the kitchen (Ich nehme keinen Zucker).
Zucker haben (colloquial) means having diabetes, not owning sugar – the context tells.
subtleties: Süßstoff is sweetener, not sugar; zuckerfrei = sugar-free.

profile.feeling: Salt and pepper on the table – and an old symbol of value.

examples.text: Die Suppe braucht noch Salz.
examples.tr: The soup still needs salt.

examples.text: Kannst du mir bitte das Salz geben?
examples.tr: Can you pass me the salt, please?

examples.text: Viele Salze lösen sich gut in Wasser.
examples.tr: Many salts dissolve well in water.

phrases.tr: to sprinkle salt into the wound
phrases.meaning: to make a painful situation worse
what makes something interesting

phrases.text: jemandem nicht das Salz in der Suppe gönnen
phrases.tr: not to grant someone the salt in his soup
phrases.meaning: to begrudge someone everything

synonyms.nuance: cooking salt, sodium chloride – textbooks and labels
table salt – the word on the packet

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German salz, from Old High German salz, from Proto-West Germanic *salt, from Proto-Germanic *saltą, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-. Compare Dutch zout, English salt, Danish salt.

funFacts: Salz, Latin sal, Ancient Greek ἅλς (modern αλάτι) and Russian соль all come from one Indo-European word; Latin salārium – the root of English salary – is linked to salt.
pitfalls: das Salz is neuter, like Greek το αλάτι; Russian соль is feminine.
Plural Salze only in chemistry (Mineralsalze) and for kinds of salt.
subtleties: salzig = salty; versalzen = too salty: Die Suppe ist versalzen.

profile.feeling: Clear and plain – and in a German restaurant usually a bottle of sparkling mineral water.

senses.def: water as an element; a body of water (sea, lake, river)

examples.text: Ich trinke jeden Tag zwei Liter Wasser.
examples.tr: I drink two litres of water every day.

examples.text: Ein Wasser, bitte!
examples.tr: A (bottle of) water, please!

examples.text: Die Kinder springen ins Wasser.
examples.tr: The children jump into the water.

phrases.meaning: quiet people often have hidden depths
to be cancelled, to fall through

phrases.text: jemandem das Wasser nicht reichen können
phrases.tr: not to be able to hand someone the water
phrases.meaning: to be no match for someone

synonyms.nuance: bottled mineral water – what you get when you order ein Wasser
sparkling mineral water – south-west Germany
tap water – ask for it by this name

etymology.text: From Middle High German waȥȥer, from Old High German waȥȥar, from Proto-West Germanic *watar, from Proto-Germanic *watōr, from Proto-Indo-European *wédōr, collective of *wódr̥. Compare Dutch water, English water, Danish vand.

funFacts: Wasser, English water, Russian вода and Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (as in hydro-) share one Indo-European root; Russian водка is literally “little water”.
pitfalls: Ordering ein Wasser brings bottled mineral water, often sparkling: ask for stilles Wasser or Leitungswasser if you want still or tap water.
das Wasser is neuter (Greek το νερό neuter; Russian вода feminine).
subtleties: Plural Wasser (servings, kinds: zwei Wasser, bitte) or Wässer (mineral waters, fruit brandies – rarer).

profile.feeling: A warm cup in the afternoon, herbal tea when you are ill, the tea ceremony of East Frisia.

examples.text: Ich trinke morgens schwarzen Tee.
examples.tr: In the morning I drink black tea.

examples.text: Möchtest du einen Tee?
examples.tr: Would you like a tea?

examples.text: Bei Erkältung trinke ich Kamillentee.
examples.tr: When I have a cold I drink camomile tea.

phrases.meaning: be patient, wait and see

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: Tee is used for real tea and for herbal infusions alike (Aufguss, “infusion”, is technical).

etymology.text: Ultimately from Hokkien 茶 (tê), probably through Dutch thee. Attested since the 17th century.

funFacts: Tea reached Europe by two roads: by sea from Hokkien tê (German Tee, English tea, Hebrew תֵּה), by land from chá (Russian чай, Turkish çay, Greek τσάι, Arabic شَاي). Mandarin says 茶 chá.
pitfalls: der Tee is masculine – like der Kaffee, der Saft, der Wein; but das Wasser, das Bier, die Milch.
Plural Tees (kinds of tea) or Tee (servings).
subtleties: Tee covers herbal infusions too: Pfefferminztee, Kamillentee, Früchtetee.
In East Frisia strong black tea is a ritual, with rock sugar (Kluntje) and cream.

profile.feeling: The morning cup and the afternoon ritual of Kaffee und Kuchen.

senses.def: afternoon coffee and cake (a small meal, especially on Sundays)

examples.text: Ich trinke morgens zwei Tassen Kaffee.
examples.tr: In the morning I drink two cups of coffee.

examples.text: Einen Kaffee, bitte!
examples.tr: A coffee, please!

examples.text: Kommt ihr am Sonntag zum Kaffee?
examples.tr: Are you coming for coffee and cake on Sunday?

phrases.meaning: that is old news
an afternoon get-together with coffee, cake and chat

synonyms.nuance: a nice little coffee – cosy
weak coffee or coffee substitute – jokey
real coffee from beans, as opposed to substitutes

etymology.text: From French café, from Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوة (qahwa). First attested in the 17th century. Doublet of Café.

funFacts: Kaffee travelled from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa) through Ottoman Turkish kahve, Italian caffè and French café; Turkish kahve, Greek καφές, Russian кофе and Hebrew קָפֶה belong to the same chain.
pitfalls: der Kaffee (the drink, in Germany usually stressed on the first syllable: KAF-fee) – das Café (a coffee house, stressed on the second: Ca-FÉ).
der Kaffee is masculine; plural Kaffees.
subtleties: Kaffee kochen is the everyday way to say “make coffee”, even with a machine.
Austria stresses Kaf-FEE and has its own coffee words: Melange, Brauner, Verlängerter.

profile.feeling: A glass of milk for children, milk in coffee – everyday and wholesome.

senses.def: milky liquid (of plants; a lotion: Reinigungsmilch)

examples.text: Die Kinder trinken jeden Morgen Milch.
examples.tr: The children drink milk every morning.

examples.text: Ich trinke Kaffee mit Milch und ohne Zucker.
examples.tr: I drink coffee with milk and no sugar.

examples.text: Wir haben keine Milch mehr.
examples.tr: We’ve run out of milk.

phrases.text: das Land, wo Milch und Honig fließen
phrases.tr: the land where milk and honey flow
phrases.meaning: a land of plenty (from the Bible)
a naive calculation that ignores the facts

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: Milch is the only word.

etymology.text: From Middle High German milch, from Old High German miluh, from Proto-West Germanic *meluk, from Proto-Germanic *meluks, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.

funFacts: die Milchstraße is the Milky Way: Greek γαλαξίας, from γάλα (milk), gave English galaxy – the same picture of milk spilled across the sky.
pitfalls: die Milch is feminine (Greek το γάλα and Russian молоко are neuter).
No plural in normal use.
subtleties: In the EU the name Milch is reserved for animal milk, so oat milk is sold as Haferdrink – though people say Hafermilch.

profile.feeling: Apple juice for the children, orange juice at breakfast – and colloquially “power”.

senses.def: sap of plants; meat juices, gravy

examples.text: Die Kinder trinken gern Apfelsaft.
examples.tr: The children like drinking apple juice.

examples.text: Ich kaufe zwei Flaschen Saft.
examples.tr: I’m buying two bottles of juice.

examples.text: Mein Handy hat keinen Saft mehr.
examples.tr: My phone’s battery is dead.

phrases.meaning: feeble, insipid

phrases.tr: to stew in one’s own juice
phrases.meaning: to be left alone with one’s problems

synonyms.nuance: nectar – a juice drink with added water and sugar, legally less fruit than Saft
juice (or wine) mixed with sparkling water – very popular in Germany

etymology.text: From Middle High German saf, saft, from Old High German saf, from Proto-West Germanic *sap (“juice, sap”).

funFacts: Saft and English sap are the same Germanic word.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: der Saft – die Säfte.
der Saft is masculine.
subtleties: Colloquially Saft is power: Der Akku hat keinen Saft mehr (the battery is flat).

examples.text: Zum Abendessen trinken wir ein Glas Wein.

examples.text: Ich kaufe eine Flasche Rotwein.
examples.tr: I’m buying a bottle of red wine.

examples.text: Am Rhein wächst viel Wein.
examples.tr: A lot of wine grows along the Rhine.

phrases.meaning: to tell someone the plain truth

phrases.tr: to preach water and drink wine
phrases.meaning: to be a hypocrite (after Heinrich Heine)
people speak the truth when drunk (Latin in vino veritas)

synonyms.nuance: “juice of the vine” – jokey or poetic
ein guter Tropfen – a good wine (lit. a good drop)

etymology.text: From Middle High German wīn, from Old High German wīn, from Proto-West Germanic *wīn, borrowed from Latin vīnum.

funFacts: Wein, English wine and Russian вино come from Latin vīnum, a cousin of Ancient Greek οἶνος (as in oenology); modern Greek says κρασί.
pitfalls: der Wein (wine) – weinen (to cry): Ich weine = I am crying.
der Wein is masculine; plural Weine.
subtleties: Wein also means the vine itself; the grape is die Weintraube.

profile.feeling: Beer gardens, the Oktoberfest, a cool beer after work – part of German culture.

senses.def: business, concern (Das ist nicht mein Bier.)

examples.text: Im Biergarten trinken wir ein Bier.
examples.tr: In the beer garden we drink a beer.

examples.text: Er kauft Bier für die Party.
examples.tr: He’s buying beer for the party.

examples.text: Das ist nicht dein Bier!
examples.tr: That’s none of your business!

phrases.meaning: that is not my business

synonyms.nuance: pilsner – the most common kind; ein Pils = a beer
Bavaria: half a litre of beer (eine Halbe)
a (nice little) beer – cosy

etymology.text: From Middle High German bier, from Old High German bior, from Proto-West Germanic *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą (“beer”). Akin to Dutch bier, English beer, Icelandic bjór.

funFacts: The Bavarian Reinheitsgebot of 1516 allowed only water, barley and hops in beer – yeast was not yet understood.
Italian birra, Greek μπίρα and Turkish bira all go back to German Bier.
pitfalls: das Bier is neuter (Greek η μπίρα feminine, Russian пиво neuter).
Ordering: zwei Bier (two glasses); zwei Biere means two kinds or two bottles.
subtleties: Beer is jokingly called flüssiges Brot (liquid bread), especially in Bavaria.

profile.feeling: Fresh rolls, jam, cheese and a boiled egg on a Sunday morning.

examples.text: Das Frühstück ist um acht Uhr.
examples.tr: Breakfast is at eight o’clock.

examples.text: Zum Frühstück esse ich Brot mit Käse.
examples.tr: For breakfast I eat bread and cheese.

examples.text: Am Sonntag machen wir ein großes Frühstück.
examples.tr: On Sunday we have a big breakfast.

phrases.text: Frühstücke wie ein Kaiser, iss zu Mittag wie ein König und zu Abend wie ein Bettelmann.
phrases.tr: Breakfast like an emperor, lunch like a king and dine like a beggar.
phrases.meaning: eat most in the morning, least in the evening

synonyms.nuance: Switzerland, colloquial
a late, long breakfast and lunch in one – an anglicism

etymology.text: From Middle High German vrüestücke (14th c.). Equivalent to früh (“early”) + Stück (“piece”, here in the sense of “bite”).

funFacts: Frühstück is an “early piece” (of bread); English breakfast breaks the night’s fast; Turkish kahvaltı comes from kahve altı, “under (before) the coffee”.
pitfalls: To “have breakfast” Germans usually use the verb frühstücken: Wir frühstücken um acht.
das Frühstück is neuter (das Stück).
subtleties: In hotels: Übernachtung mit Frühstück = bed and breakfast.

profile.feeling: The hot midday meal – in many families and schools the main meal of the day.

examples.text: Das Mittagessen ist fertig!
examples.tr: Lunch is ready!

examples.text: Was gibt es heute zum Mittagessen?
examples.tr: What’s for lunch today?

examples.text: Ich koche das Mittagessen für die Kinder.
examples.tr: I’m cooking lunch for the children.

phrases.meaning: a lunchtime greeting among colleagues (also “enjoy your meal”)

synonyms.nuance: Was gibt’s zu Mittag? – the meal named by the time
an anglicism, business and city life
a restaurant’s set lunch menu

etymology.text: From Mittag (“midday”) + Essen (“meal”).

funFacts: Greek μεσημεριανό (from μεσημέρι, midday) and Turkish öğle yemeği (noon meal) name lunch by the time of day, just like Mittagessen.
pitfalls: das Mittagessen is neuter, like das Essen (the meal); plural Mittagessen.
Mittag = noon, Mittagessen = the meal, Nachmittag = afternoon.
subtleties: At lunchtime colleagues greet each other with Mahlzeit! (“mealtime!”).

profile.feeling: The evening meal with the family – warm or, in the old style, bread and cold cuts.

examples.text: Das Abendessen ist um sieben.
examples.tr: Dinner is at seven.

examples.text: Wir laden Freunde zum Abendessen ein.
examples.tr: We’re inviting friends to dinner.

examples.text: Zum Abendessen gibt es Suppe und Brot.
examples.tr: For dinner there’s soup and bread.

synonyms.nuance: north and east: a simple, mostly cold evening meal of bread and toppings
Austria
Switzerland, colloquial
a festive or business dinner – an anglicism

etymology.text: From Abend (“evening”) + Essen (“meal”).

funFacts: German names its meals by the time of day – Frühstück (early), Mittagessen (midday), Abendessen (evening) – and Greek does the same: πρωινό, μεσημεριανό, βραδινό.
pitfalls: das Abendessen is neuter; plural Abendessen.
Abend (evening) is masculine, but the compound takes the gender of its last part: das Essen → das Abendessen.
subtleties: Guten Appetit! is said before any meal; Abendbrot hints at a simple cold supper.
